strengths: The proposed reduction from the Childs et al. glued-trees oracle problem is conceptually strong and, if completed correctly, would establish a significant unconditional exponential query separation for a central linear-algebra problem.

The hard instance is especially compelling: the matrix is real symmetric, has at most four nonzeros per row and column, has polylogarithmic condition number in the matrix dimension, and uses the simple right-hand side e1.

The manuscript carefully matches the quantum output model with the classical task of sampling from an approximate solution, avoiding the inappropriate comparison with explicitly outputting the entire solution vector.

The construction of M and the simulation of entry and row/column sampling access using graph-oracle queries are intuitive and largely plausible. The subsequent parameter translation correctly aims to turn a 2^(n/6) graph-query lower bound into an N^(1/12) linear-system lower bound.
The motivation for choosing lambda just above sqrt(8), and the analysis relating the solution mass at the second root to the precision and condition number, provide useful technical insight.

The paper is generally self-contained and readable for a theoretical submission. It gives explicit constructions and derivations, so no experimental code or unavailable data are needed for reproduction. The work raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The proof of the central spectral Lemma 1 contains a fundamental gap. Observation 2 claims that every eigenvalue of A has a nonzero layered eigenvector, but its construction averages an arbitrary eigenvector over each level. All of these averages can be zero, yielding the zero vector rather than an eigenvector. Equitable-partition averaging only preserves the projection onto the layered subspace; it does not imply that every eigenspace intersects that subspace nontrivially. Consequently, the subsequent recurrence analyzes only layered eigenvectors and does not rule out non-layered eigenvalues in (sqrt(8), 3-2^(-n)].

Lemma 1 is essential: without excluding those non-layered eigenvalues, lambda I-A may have a singular value much smaller than gamma, so the claimed O(log^2 N) condition number and hence the exponential quantum-classical separation do not follow. A separate bound on the spectrum orthogonal to the layered subspace may exist, but it is absent and would require substantial new argument rather than a local algebraic correction.

The SQ(M) simulation is not fully specified. The access definition includes querying every row/column norm and the norms associated with r(M) and c(M), but the simulation only explicitly discusses entry queries and sampling. These quantities appear recoverable with constant oracle cost or from known graph statistics, yet this should be stated and included in the query accounting.

The replacement of the exact norm-weighted distribution for sampling rows and columns by a uniform distribution is argued only through conditioning on not selecting a root. A formal coupling or total-variation calculation is needed, including the discrepancy between the true and simulated probabilities of the two root rows; the stated 2T·2^(-2n) loss is not rigorously derived as written.

The QIC problem statement does not clearly specify algorithmic failure probability, whether the approximation vector may depend on internal randomness, or the success convention for randomized preprocessing. These details matter when converting the sampler into an algorithm contradicting the bounded-success glued-trees lower bound.

The significance and originality would be very high if the theorem were established, but the current manuscript cannot support its headline claim because the missing spectral argument sits at the core of the proof. The result also applies only at the stringent precision epsilon=O(log^(-2.5) N), which limits its reach and deserves clearer treatment as a limitation.

The related-work discussion and bibliography appear to stop around 2024. For an ICML 2026 submission, the claim of being the first such separation requires an updated comparison with relevant 2025-2026 work.

strengths: The problem is significant: an unconditional exponential separation between quantum and quantum-inspired classical algorithms for sparse, well-conditioned linear systems would be an important theoretical result.

The proposed reduction from the Childs et al. glued-trees oracle problem is conceptually appealing. The construction is sparse, uses the simple right-hand side e1, and clearly explains how the claimed n^(1/12) lower bound follows from the exponential glued-trees bound.

The exposition is generally self-contained and provides useful intuition for choosing lambda near sqrt(8), including the tradeoff between conditioning and probability mass at the second root. No material research-ethics concerns arise.
weaknesses: The central spectral argument is invalid. Observation 2 claims that every eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix has a layered eigenvector. Averaging an eigenvector within each level does preserve the eigenvalue only when the averaged vector is nonzero; for eigenvectors whose coordinates sum to zero on every level, the result is the zero vector. Such non-layered eigenspaces are entirely possible for this equitable level partition. The proof overlooks this case.

Consequently, Section 2.2 analyzes only the spectrum on the low-dimensional layered subspace and does not rule out non-layered eigenvalues in (sqrt(8), 3-2^(-n)]. Lemma 1 is therefore unproved. This is decisive because Lemma 1 supplies the lower bound on the smallest singular value of B=lambda I-A and hence the claimed polylogarithmic condition number.

The claimed universal form of Lemma 1 is also doubtful for an arbitrary alternating cycle: the cycle can be arranged to create highly structured or weakly connected regions, whereas no expansion or non-layered spectral analysis is provided. If the intended statement is probabilistic for a uniformly random cycle, it requires a new high-probability spectral theorem and an argument that conditioning on the good event preserves the glued-trees query lower bound.

Without the condition-number guarantee, the construction does not establish an exponential quantum/classical separation: the quantum benchmark depends directly on kappa, so the paper's headline theorem and significance claim do not follow from the current proof.

The manuscript is readable, but its repeated assertion that Lemma 1 has been proved obscures the distinction between the quotient/layered spectrum and the full adjacency spectrum. Reproducibility is limited by this mathematical gap rather than by missing code or experiments; this is a theorem paper, but independent verification of the central claim fails at Observation 2. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations discussion and presents the result as unconditional without acknowledging the required spectral assumption.

strengths: The claimed contribution is highly significant: an unconditional exponential query-complexity separation between quantum and quantum-inspired classical algorithms for linear systems, with 4-sparse matrices, polylogarithmic condition number, and explicit precision dependence.

The reduction from the glued-trees oracle problem is conceptually clean. The manuscript explicitly constructs M, explains how sampling/query access is simulated, tracks the simulation error at the two exceptional root rows, and translates the parameters to an Ω(N^{1/12}) lower bound for an N-dimensional system.

The exposition is generally strong. It carefully motivates why λ must lie just above √8, distinguishes full-vector output from solution-distribution sampling, compares against relevant classical and quantum benchmarks, and supplies detailed algebra for the solution-amplitude bound.

As a theoretical paper, it is reasonably self-contained and does not inherently require code or empirical artifacts for reproducibility. The construction and parameter choices are stated explicitly. I found no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: There is a fundamental gap in Observation 2, on which Lemma 1 and the main theorem depend. Averaging an arbitrary eigenvector over every level does produce a layered vector w satisfying Aw=λw, but w may be the zero vector: an eigenvector can have zero sum on every level. The proof never establishes that this projection is nonzero. Thus it does not show that every eigenvalue has a layered eigenvector, and the subsequent analysis only rules out unwanted eigenvalues within the layered subspace.

Because Lemma 1 is used to exclude adjacency eigenvalues in (√8,3−2^{−n}], this gap directly invalidates the asserted lower bound on the smallest singular value of B=λI−A. Without a separate spectral analysis of the non-layered subspace, B could have an eigenvalue much closer to zero, destroying the O(log²N) condition-number guarantee and hence the advertised quantum/classical separation. Repairing this appears to require a substantial new argument, not a local clarification.

The paper should distinguish more sharply between a separation for its oracle-access, sample-output formulation and a broad practical quantum advantage for machine learning. The hard family is specially constructed, the output is only a sample from the squared solution coordinates, and the guarantee requires inverse-polylogarithmic precision. These are legitimate theoretical choices, but they limit the reach of the introductory framing.

There is no dedicated limitations discussion, and the manuscript does not flag the dependence of the result on the strong spectral claim about the glued-trees graph. The presentation and originality are promising, but they cannot compensate for the unsupported central condition-number claim. A complete proof controlling all non-layered eigenvectors is necessary before the result can be accepted.

strengths: The paper addresses an important foundational question and proposes a potentially significant exponential separation for linear-system solving under the sampling-and-query access model used by quantum-inspired algorithms.

The core fixed-k construction is conceptually strong: combining the HHL circuit-to-linear-system reduction with k-Forrelation plausibly produces real symmetric, 3-sparse instances with polylogarithmic condition number, while allowing classical simulation of each sampling/query operation.
The treatment of approximate solutions is useful and reasonably clear. The total-variation calculation shows how relative ℓ2 error in the solution vector affects the output sampling distribution.
The access model, output requirement, quantum benchmark, and relevant prior work are explained carefully. The manuscript is generally readable and professionally presented.
As a theoretical paper, it does not require an experimental artifact; much of the construction is explicit, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: A key claim in the random-walk proof is invalid as written. Observation 2 asserts that averaging any eigenvector within graph levels yields a nonzero layered eigenvector of the same eigenvalue. The averaged vector can instead be identically zero when the original eigenvector is orthogonal to the layer-constant subspace. The calculation only proves that the projection is either a layered eigenvector or zero. Consequently, the argument does not exclude non-layered eigenvectors in the claimed spectral interval, leaving Lemma 1, the condition-number bound, and the entire random-walk reduction unsupported.

The k-Forrelation proof does not establish Theorem 1 with its stated uniform quantifiers. The cited lower bound is invoked only when k is constant, the required repetition contributes a 2^{O(k)} factor, and the constructed dimension is O(kn2^n) with condition number O(kn). For variable k, this condition number is not shown to be O(log N), and the hidden k-dependent losses are not shown to yield a universal constant times N^{1-1/k} for every pair N,k. The final sentence claiming that rescaling k by two resolves all these issues is insufficient.

These are central soundness problems rather than cosmetic omissions. A credible fixed-constant-k exponential separation may remain after weakening the theorem and relying only on the Forrelation construction, but the substantially stronger theorem currently advertised is not proved.

Reproducibility of the theoretical result is weakened by the absence of a precise quoted k-Forrelation lower-bound theorem, including its allowed k regime and constant dependence, followed by a complete parameter translation to the final matrix dimension, precision, condition number, and query bound.

There are smaller consistency and presentation issues: Section 2 refers to an alternative reduction from Simon's problem although Section 3 uses k-Forrelation, and the claimed quantum runtime of log(n) log log(n) is not clearly reconciled with the theorem's independent precision parameter. The statement that the result holds at constant precision is valid only after fixing k and should be qualified accordingly.

The paper contains no explicit limitations discussion. This is not itself a reason for rejection, but acknowledging that the first reduction needs control of the non-layered spectrum and that the second argument is established only in a fixed-k regime would materially improve the accuracy of the claims.

strengths: The fixed-k Forrelation/HHL construction is promising and, if repaired and stated with appropriate parameter restrictions, appears capable of establishing a meaningful exponential query-complexity separation. The sparse symmetric linear-system construction and reduction from solution sampling to circuit-output sampling are technically interesting.

The topic is significant: an unconditional separation between quantum and quantum-inspired classical algorithms for linear systems would directly address an important question raised by dequantization results.

The manuscript is generally well organized and motivates the matrix constructions clearly. The second reduction is reasonably self-contained, and the theoretical nature of the work means that the absence of code or experiments is not itself a reproducibility problem.
The work appears original in combining Forrelation with the HHL circuit-to-linear-system reduction to study quantum-inspired sampling access. I found no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The random-walk reduction contains a fundamental proof gap. Observation 2 claims that every eigenvalue has a nonzero layered eigenvector by averaging an arbitrary eigenvector within levels. Such averaging can produce the zero vector; invariance of the layered subspace does not imply that every eigenvalue occurs in it. Consequently, the proof of Lemma 1 does not exclude non-layered eigenvectors with eigenvalues in the critical interval, undermining the condition-number analysis and the claimed new spectral insight.

The Forrelation reduction is explicitly analyzed only when k is constant, but Theorem 1 quantifies over every pair of integers n,k with a universal constant and claims condition number O(log n). In the presented construction, the circuit length and condition number scale as O(kn), while the matrix dimension is only O(kn·2^n). Thus the claimed O(log N) condition number is justified for constant k, not arbitrary k. The absorption of logarithmic and 2^{O(k)} factors into an N^{1-1/k} lower bound likewise requires unstated restrictions relating k and N. This is a central theorem-level overclaim rather than a cosmetic omission.

The total-variation calculation in the approximation argument contains an incorrect equality: converting the denominator from ||x||² to ||x-tilde||² requires multiplying by ||x||²/||x-tilde||², whereas the manuscript uses the reciprocal. An O(epsilon) bound is probably recoverable by a standard normalization argument, but the written proof is invalid.

The headline quantum-runtime comparison suppresses the dependence on k through epsilon when k is not constant, reinforcing the mismatch between the theorem's quantifiers and the regime actually analyzed.

The paper does not adequately discuss the limitations of its oracle/query model or the restricted parameter regime supported by the proof. Although the fixed-k result could still be valuable, the manuscript currently presents a substantially stronger conclusion than its analysis establishes. Because both advertised reductions contain significant unresolved issues, other researchers cannot yet reliably build on the main theorem.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper targets an important open question and gives a compelling route to an unconditional exponential separation between quantum and quantum-inspired classical algorithms for sparse linear systems.

Soundness: The k-Forrelation reduction combines the HHL circuit-to-linear-system construction with classical query lower bounds in a conceptually strong way. It explicitly addresses sparsity, symmetry, conditioning, simulation of sampling/query access, and error from approximate solutions.

Robustness: Two substantially different reductions are presented. The k-Forrelation argument is independent of the random-walk construction and appears to establish a meaningful exponential separation for every fixed choice of k.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear, well motivated, and unusually helpful about the intuition behind its constructions. The comparison with prior QIC lower bounds and quantum upper bounds is informative.

Reproducibility: This is a theoretical contribution requiring no experimental artifacts; most constructions and calculations are provided in detail, and the relevant oracle-access model is formally defined.
Ethics: The work raises no apparent research-ethics or societal-risk concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: Observation 2 is false as stated. Averaging an arbitrary eigenvector over graph levels can produce the zero vector, so a nonzero eigenvector need not yield a nonzero layered eigenvector with the same eigenvalue. The proof only notes that the original real eigenvector is nonzero and never establishes that its level averages are nonzero. Consequently, the proof of Lemma 1—and therefore the random-walk reduction relying on its spectral gap—is incomplete.

Soundness: The k-Forrelation argument is explicitly analyzed for constant k, whereas Theorem 1 quantifies over all integers n,k with one universal constant c. In the construction, the circuit length is T=(k+1)n+k, so the HHL matrix has condition number O(kn), not O(n)=O(log N) uniformly in k. The manuscript invokes constant k and then concludes the fully quantified theorem without resolving this dependence.

Soundness/reproducibility: The transition from an internal dimension N=Theta(kn2^n) and a lower bound containing logarithmic losses to an arbitrary target dimension and Omega(N^{1-1/k}) is summarized only as 'rescaling k by a factor 2.' Padding, parameter ranges of the cited k-Forrelation bound, constants, and the simultaneous effects on precision and condition number should be stated rigorously.

Presentation: The abstract and contribution statement present Theorem 1 without qualifying the two proof gaps above. The paper also lacks an explicit limitations discussion distinguishing the apparently supported fixed-k separation from the stronger uniform-in-k statement.

Overall: The fixed-k k-Forrelation result appears novel and important, but the strongest stated theorem is not established as written, and one complete alternative proof contains a fundamental projection error. A revision that weakens the theorem to the rigorously supported parameter regime or supplies the missing uniform analysis, and repairs or removes the random-walk spectral argument, is needed before acceptance.
